California lawmakers resurrect $7.5 billion research bond to counter federal cuts
By Tarini Mehta
August 28, 2026 5:55 PM
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, delivers remarks during a debate at the Capitol in Sacramento on Friday, June 13, 2025. Wiener authored a bill that seeks to place a $7.5 billion bond for scientific research funding on the ballot.
DANIEL HEUER
dheuer@sacbee.com
A multibillion dollar bond proposal that sought to fund scientific research (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316251545.html) amid federal funding cuts failed to meet the June deadline to secure its place as a statewide measure on the November ballot. Lawmakers resurrected the language just before the close of the legislative session this week, aiming now to present the measure to voters in the March 2028 primary election.
At a news conference Friday, Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, announced that the governor along with Senate and Assembly leadership had reached a deal on the science bond bill he authored in January. The latest amendment Thursday night shrunk the funding it would provide for science and health research from $23 billion to $7.5 billion. Now, the bill must survive the Legislature before it concludes on Aug. 31 and receive the governor’s signature to advance — steps that Wiener said he was “cautiously optimistic” about.
“This represents a major effort by California to stand up against the attack on science by the Trump administration, which is methodically tearing down federal support for scientific research, and to really triple down on California’s global leadership,” Wiener said. “This is a big win for the millions of Californians that rely on scientific advancement to cure diseases, prevent diseases, treat diseases, improve people’s health and quality of life, to protect people from wildfires, to build the next generation of agricultural innovations, to lower the cost of food, and so on and so forth.”
Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895) is an effort to backfill federal funding cuts to research under the Trump administration through a bond program. A bond is a type of long-term borrowing to raise money for various purposes. The state obtains the money by selling bonds to investors and agrees to repay it, with interest, per a specified schedule. The proposed program would be used to finance grants and loans to fund research and construct, operate and maintain facilities for that work.
The bill — through the ballot measure — would establish the California Foundation for Science and Health Research to award grants and loans to public or private research companies, universities and organizations in the fields of biomedical, disease prevention, wildfire prevention, and climate, among others. The legislation also mandates that 10% of the funds be set aside for a state research program modeled after the federal Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and $1 billion be available to the University of California and California State University for construction of research facilities.
The measure has nearly 50 co-authors and strong organizational support, including from the UC, CSU and Stanford University. It is backed by UAW 4811, which represents 60,000 scientists and academic researchers at the University of California.
Loading…
Shortly after Wiener announced the deal on his bill, Nobel laureates Jennifer Doudna and Randy Schekman issued statements supporting the UC-sponsored legislation. Both UC Berkeley professors, the scientists said SB 895 was critical to California’s research infrastructure and advancement of scientific breakthroughs that improve lives and drive growth.
“California’s strength and ingenuity depends on its ability to turn bold ideas into solutions to our most pressing problems,” Schekman said. “That’s why we need to invest in research and continue building on our nation-leading enterprise at UC. SB 895 will help protect the people and discoveries that drive billions of dollars in economic activity and improve lives across our state.”
While Wiener’s science bond is clawing its way onto the March 2028 ballot, a separate but similar initiative will be voted on by Californians this November. If approved by voters,Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316259099.html) will authorize $8.4 billion in state bonds for California-based public and nonprofit universities and medical research institutions to conduct immunology and immunotherapy research.
Half the funds would be allocated to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the rest for research grants to other public or nonprofit institutions. In July, CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) reported that the measure was written in a way that likely predetermines the single institute that will receive half the funds. That institute is the UCLA-affiliated California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. At the news conference Friday, Wiener said he was not worried about Proposition 38 hurting his proposed bond’s chances.
“That ballot measure primarily funds one particular institute. It’s not a broad science policy funding measure, and so it’s just very different, and I don’t view it as a competitor,” he said.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).

Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)

It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.

Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.

Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.

Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.
About Opinion
Guest opinions in Open Forum and Insight are produced by writers with expertise, personal experience or original insights on a subject of interest to our readers. Their views do not necessarily reflect the opinion of The Chronicle editorial board, which is committed to providing a diversity of ideas to our readership.
Read more about our transparency and ethics policies (https://www.sfchronicle.com/standards/)
And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.
Emily Hoeven is a columnist and editorial writer for the Opinion section.

Who they are
Emily Hoeven is an opinion columnist and a member of the Chronicle’s editorial board. Her work has sparked changes to San Francisco and California law and has been honored by the National Headliner Awards, the Poynter Institute and the Best of the West competition among others.
The former author of CalMatters’ daily WhatMatters newsletter on California politics and policy, Emily got her start writing opinion columns for the Mercury News and the Daily Pennsylvanian and reported for papers in Montana and Utah. Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative
Updated October 28, 2026
Proposition 38 on the 2026 California ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) will provide vitally needed funding to cure and prevent devastating diseases that impact millions of Californians, including cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's (https://yeson38.com/faq/).
Key reasons to vote YES on Prop 38, the Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative:
Helps offset federal cuts to medical research
Prop 38 responds to federal funding cuts and uncertainty (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) that are delaying life-saving medical research.
Dedicated funding for cancer, Alzheimer's and heart disease research
Half of all funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) are dedicated specifically to research into cures for Alzheimer's, cancer and heart disease.
Fosters collaboration between leading scientists and physicians
Grants are overseen by an Advisory Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) of leading scientists, doctors and researchers in the field of immunology.
Mandates strong accountability and transparency
State administrative costs are limited to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), with public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
Designed to pay for itself – including interest
Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest.
Requires 20% discount on treatments and cures for Californians
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) below the national average.

Prop 38 Frequently Asked Questions
What does a YES vote on Prop 38 mean?
A YES vote on Prop 38 means California will support $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology research (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at California universities and nonprofit research institutions to find cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease and other devastating diseases in our lifetime. Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself, with 10% of proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies developed from Prop 38 funding returned to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm). Additionally, California patients will get a 20% discount on the cures it helps create (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).

Where will the research funded by Prop 38 happen?
Medical research funded by Prop 38 will be conducted here in California at leading universities and medical research institutions (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) that are well-qualified to conduct breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research.
That may include University of California campuses, such as UCLA, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, UC San Francisco, UC Irvine, UC Davis, and UC Riverside; private non-profit universities, such as Stanford, USC and Caltech; and non-profit research institutions such as City of Hope, Cedars-Sinai, and Sanford Burnham Prebys, among others.
No funds from Prop 38 can be awarded to pharmaceutical companies or other for-profit corporations. (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)

Will Prop 38 make medical treatments more affordable for Californians?
Yes. Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount below the national average (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf). That affordability protection is written directly into the measure — it’s not optional.

Prop 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers (https://yeson38.com/myths-vs-facts/#can-california-afford). Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.

How does Prop 38 ensure oversight and accountability?
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits.

01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.

One more question
Why less sunlight for billions in public money?
Despite promises of accountability, the selected institute would not be treated as a public agency under key California transparency and ethics laws, including the Public Records Act, open-meeting requirements and the Political Reform Act.
Public money should come with full public accountability.
Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

California lawmakers resurrect $7.5 billion research bond to counter federal cuts
By Tarini Mehta
August 28, 2026 5:55 PM
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, delivers remarks during a debate at the Capitol in Sacramento on Friday, June 13, 2025. Wiener authored a bill that seeks to place a $7.5 billion bond for scientific research funding on the ballot.
DANIEL HEUER
dheuer@sacbee.com
A multibillion dollar bond proposal that sought to fund scientific research (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316251545.html) amid federal funding cuts failed to meet the June deadline to secure its place as a statewide measure on the November ballot. Lawmakers resurrected the language just before the close of the legislative session this week, aiming now to present the measure to voters in the March 2028 primary election.
At a news conference Friday, Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, announced that the governor along with Senate and Assembly leadership had reached a deal on the science bond bill he authored in January. The latest amendment Thursday night shrunk the funding it would provide for science and health research from $23 billion to $7.5 billion. Now, the bill must survive the Legislature before it concludes on Aug. 31 and receive the governor’s signature to advance — steps that Wiener said he was “cautiously optimistic” about.
“This represents a major effort by California to stand up against the attack on science by the Trump administration, which is methodically tearing down federal support for scientific research, and to really triple down on California’s global leadership,” Wiener said. “This is a big win for the millions of Californians that rely on scientific advancement to cure diseases, prevent diseases, treat diseases, improve people’s health and quality of life, to protect people from wildfires, to build the next generation of agricultural innovations, to lower the cost of food, and so on and so forth.”
Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895) is an effort to backfill federal funding cuts to research under the Trump administration through a bond program. A bond is a type of long-term borrowing to raise money for various purposes. The state obtains the money by selling bonds to investors and agrees to repay it, with interest, per a specified schedule. The proposed program would be used to finance grants and loans to fund research and construct, operate and maintain facilities for that work.
The bill — through the ballot measure — would establish the California Foundation for Science and Health Research to award grants and loans to public or private research companies, universities and organizations in the fields of biomedical, disease prevention, wildfire prevention, and climate, among others. The legislation also mandates that 10% of the funds be set aside for a state research program modeled after the federal Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and $1 billion be available to the University of California and California State University for construction of research facilities.
The measure has nearly 50 co-authors and strong organizational support, including from the UC, CSU and Stanford University. It is backed by UAW 4811, which represents 60,000 scientists and academic researchers at the University of California.
Loading…
Shortly after Wiener announced the deal on his bill, Nobel laureates Jennifer Doudna and Randy Schekman issued statements supporting the UC-sponsored legislation. Both UC Berkeley professors, the scientists said SB 895 was critical to California’s research infrastructure and advancement of scientific breakthroughs that improve lives and drive growth.
“California’s strength and ingenuity depends on its ability to turn bold ideas into solutions to our most pressing problems,” Schekman said. “That’s why we need to invest in research and continue building on our nation-leading enterprise at UC. SB 895 will help protect the people and discoveries that drive billions of dollars in economic activity and improve lives across our state.”
While Wiener’s science bond is clawing its way onto the March 2028 ballot, a separate but similar initiative will be voted on by Californians this November. If approved by voters,Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316259099.html) will authorize $8.4 billion in state bonds for California-based public and nonprofit universities and medical research institutions to conduct immunology and immunotherapy research.
Half the funds would be allocated to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the rest for research grants to other public or nonprofit institutions. In July, CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) reported that the measure was written in a way that likely predetermines the single institute that will receive half the funds. That institute is the UCLA-affiliated California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. At the news conference Friday, Wiener said he was not worried about Proposition 38 hurting his proposed bond’s chances.
“That ballot measure primarily funds one particular institute. It’s not a broad science policy funding measure, and so it’s just very different, and I don’t view it as a competitor,” he said.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)

It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

Myths vs Facts
Get the facts on Prop 38. Learn what the initiative will do and find answers to some of the most common questions about Prop 38.
Updated October 26, 2026
Can California afford Prop 38?
Fact: Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#accountability). 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go back to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), covering both the principal and the interest of the bonds. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most prevalent diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses for Californians by tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses and lower insurance premiums.
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits. Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on saving lives.
For the millions of families that are facing life-threatening and life-altering diseases that take away our loved ones, we can’t afford NOT to invest in promising cures .
Why does California need Prop 38 when the federal government funds medical research too?
Fact: Prop 38 responds to massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty that are shutting down life-saving medical research (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) at California universities and research institutes. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can’t afford to wait.
Prop 38 creates a stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts to accelerate the pace of discoveries to help the tens of millions of patients fighting cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other debilitating diseases.
Prop 38 will make California a national leader in breakthrough medical research , fostering collaboration between leading California-based universities, scientists and physicians.
Prop 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs . Scientific research has become a critical economic engine in California, and studies show (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf) that each dollar invested in medical research returns three dollars back into our state’s economy.
Does half of Prop 38 funding go to one research institute?
Fact: Half of Prop 38 funding will support a world-class nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California with access to leading scientists, technology, laboratory equipment, patients and clinical trials necessary to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.
The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy will very likely apply for funding and meet qualification requirements. However, state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific named institute (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-12/) but can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. Ultimately, the California Department of Public Health is charged with determining which institute receives the funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm).
Will scientists or politicians decide which research Prop 38 funds?
Fact: Under Prop 38, scientists and researchers oversee a competitive process to ensure the most qualified research with life-saving potential is awarded funding. Prop 38 establishes an Advisory and Accountability Research Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), composed of members from seven University of California campuses and 10 – 15 members from California nonprofit universities and academic and research institutions. Each member of the council will be a physician, scientist or researcher with demonstrated experience in the field of immunology and immunotherapy.
Should the private sector fund this research instead of Prop 38?
Fact: Public funding like Prop 38 is vital to support medical research. More than 99% of new FDA-approved drugs from 2010 to 2019 were built on publicly funded research. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2804378) Prop 38 builds on this proven model by supporting universities and nonprofit researchers to move discoveries from the lab to patients faster and more cost-effectively.
Will the people funding Prop 38 benefit financially?
Fact: Prop 38 is funded by a doctor and philanthropists who will not benefit financially. Only public universities and nonprofit research institutions in California are eligible to receive research funding.
YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocates (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses AssociationCalifornia, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson’s Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, as well as patients, doctors and researchers because it will accelerate life-saving cures. This is a publicly accountable, voter-approved bond.

Dear Attorney General Becerra:
Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed statutory initiative
(A.G. File No. 19-0022, Amendment #1) that would authorize $5.5 billion in general obligation
bonds for stem cell research and enact various changes to the California Institute for
Regenerative Medicine (CIRM).
Background
Researchers Use Stem Cells to Study and Treat Various Diseases. Stem cells are certain
types of cells that exist within humans. Researchers are interested in these types of cells for their
potential to regenerate lost cells, tissues, and organs. The field of medicine that uses stem cells
and other techniques for this purpose is known as “regenerative medicine.” One well-known
example of a regenerative medicine procedure is a bone marrow transplant. Under this
procedure, the bone marrow of a donor (which contains stem cells) is transferred to another
patient to replenish lost blood cells, typically due to certain types of cancer. Scientists are
researching the use of stem cells to treat many other diseases and health conditions.
Voters Established State Stem Cell Research Program. In 2004, voters approved
Proposition 71, which gave researchers in California a constitutional right to conduct stem cell
research. The measure also created a new state program to fund stem cell research projects,
research facilities, and other related activities. In tandem, it created a new entity, CIRM, to
administer the program. The measure also established a CIRM oversight structure, which
includes (1) a 29-member governing board responsible for making funding decisions and
adopting relevant policies, (2) three working groups responsible for advising the governing
board, and (3) a five-member committee responsible for providing independent oversight over
CIRM’s finances.
Voters Approved $3 Billion in General Obligation Bonds for Stem Cell Program. To fund
stem cell grants and CIRM’s operations, the measure authorized the state to sell general
obligation bonds. State general obligation bonds are a form of borrowing. The state sells the
bonds to investors, and the proceeds of these sales provide funding to CIRM. The state sells the
Hon. Xavier Becerra 2 December 2, 2019
bonds when CIRM needs the funds (typically once a round of grant awardees has been selected).
Once the bonds are sold to investors, the state begins repaying the investors with interest by
making annual payments over time. Proposition 71 did not specify the length of the repayment
period for each bond issuance, but the state tended to repay the bonds over ten years.
Proposition 71 bonds were taxable and a ten-year repayment period is common for these types of
bonds. (For taxable bonds, the interest that investors earn is not exempt from federal taxes.)
CIRM Has Spent Nearly All Available Funds. As Figure 1 shows, bonds issued under
Proposition 71 have comprised virtually all of CIRM’s funding, with a relatively small amount
of funding coming from investment income, private donations, and other sources. CIRM has
spent most of the available funding on grants, with smaller amounts spent on CIRM’s operations
and bond costs (discussed later in this letter). As of October 2019, all but $132 million of
CIRM’s funding has been spent. According to CIRM staff, the remaining funding will be used
primarily to oversee active grants.
Grants Have Funded Several Different Purposes. As Figure 2 (on the next page) shows,
CIRM has awarded about 75 percent of grant funds for specific research projects, including
clinical trials. The remaining 25 percent of grant funds have supported research facility
construction and equipment, related activities (for example, establishing a network of
laboratories dedicated to implementing human clinical trials), and various education initiatives
(for example, research internships for undergraduate students). The University of California has
received the greatest amount of grant funding, followed by nonprofit universities and institutions
(such as Stanford University).
CIRM Is Reducing Staffing Levels. Under Proposition 71, CIRM could spend no more than
3 percent of bond proceeds on its general administrative costs and no more than 3 percent to
Hon. Xavier Becerra 3 December 2, 2019
administer grants. At full implementation, CIRM reports having over 50 full-time equivalent
staff. As it nears the end of its programmatic funding, it has reduced operations. Currently,
CIRM employs 35 full-time equivalent staff.
CIRM Used a Small Share of Bond Proceeds for Interest Payments. Typically, the state
makes regular payments on general obligation bonds from the state General Fund. Proposition 71
required the state to take a somewhat different approach. For the first five years after receiving
voter approval, the measure required CIRM to repay interest using the bonds’ proceeds.
According to CIRM, a total of about $70 million of bond proceeds were spent on interest costs
from 2004 through 2009. In 2010, the state began paying the remaining principal and interest
from the General Fund. Currently, the state is spending $327 million annually from the General
Fund to make debt payments on Proposition 71 bonds.
Small Amount of Funding Spent on Bond Issuance Costs. Typically, certain administrative
and legal costs are associated with a bond issuance. Proposition 71 specified that bond proceeds
were to cover these administrative costs. CIRM reports using $2.6 million in bond proceeds for
these costs.
Grant Recipients Have Contributed Matching Funds to Their Projects. Many of CIRM’s
programs require a match from grant recipients. The amount of funding that applicants must
match varies by program. To cover their match, grants recipients can rely on a number of
different fund sources, including philanthropic donations, federal grants, and industry
contributions. Many recipients raise more funding than required. According to CIRM, grant
recipients report collecting a combined $4.1 billion in matching funds since 2004.

Grantees Are Required to Share Invention-Related Income With the State. Some stem cell
research is expected to lead to new inventions, including new medical technology and
treatments. Proposition 71 established an expectation that grant recipients share a portion of the
income resulting from licensing or commercializing these inventions with the state. The state’s
share of the income is deposited into the state General Fund (the state’s main operating account),
which is available to support any state program. Over the years, CIRM’s governing board has
developed specific revenue-sharing policies. Since 2004, grant recipients have contributed
$352,560 in total invention-related income to the state.
Proposal
Authorizes $5.5 Billion in Bonds for Stem Cell Activities. The proposed measure would
authorize new bonds to fund additional grants and CIRM operations. As Figure 3 (see next
page) shows, the measure limits the amount of funds CIRM can spend on its operations. In
addition, the measure sets aside a portion of bond funds for certain grant programs, such as
grants for research projects that are aimed at developing treatments and cures for diseases
affecting the brain and nervous system. For a few of these programs, CIRM’s governing board
would be required to prioritize grant applications that offer matching funds and ensure grant
awardees are distributed across the state.
Establishes Certain Rules and Guidelines Relating to the Bonds. The measure would limit
the amount of bonds the state could sell each year, with the goal of spreading bond sales over at
least a ten-year period. For the first five years after the measure is enacted, bond proceeds would
cover any interest payments on the issued bonds. Beginning January 1, 2026, the state would pay
all remaining debt from the General Fund. The State Treasurer would decide the period over
which to repay the bonds, with a maximum repayment period of 40 years.
Makes Numerous Changes to CIRM. The measure would make various changes to CIRM’s
programs and governance structure. Figure 4 (see page 6) summarizes these changes. One
notable change would be to refocus some of CIRM’s efforts toward improving patient access to
stem cell treatments. Under the measure, CIRM would be allowed to hire up to 15 full-time
equivalent employees to research and develop ways to improve access to treatments. A new
working group of national experts would advise CIRM’s governing board on ways to improve
access and affordability. Furthermore, the measure would require any revenue earned from
revenue-sharing agreements to be used to offset patient costs for regenerative medicine
treatments.
Fiscal Effects
Total Estimated State Costs of $7.8 Billion. For the purposes of estimating the cost of the
measure, we assume the bonds are sold over an initial ten-year period—the minimum period
required by the measure. We assume each bond is repaid over 15 years, resulting in a total
repayment period of 25 years. Though the typical repayment period for taxable bonds is
ten years, we assume a somewhat longer period given the measure specifies that the Treasurer
could decide to stretch repayments up to 40 years. Under these assumptions, we estimate the
measure would cost a total of $7.8 billion—$5.5 billion in principal and $2.3 billion in interest.
The average annual payment over the 25-year period would be $310 million. The costs would be

higher or lower than our estimates depending on factors such as the interest rate and the period of
time over which the bonds are repaid.
Likely Low Hundreds of Millions in Interest Payments Paid by Bond Proceeds. Under the
measure, a portion of the $2.3 billion interest cost would be paid by the bond proceeds. The
portion of interest repaid from the bond proceeds would depend on the timing of when the state
begins issuing bonds and the interest rate at which the bonds are sold. Were the state to begin
issuing bonds shortly after approval of the measure, CIRM would likely make interest payments
totaling in the low hundreds of millions of dollars from bond proceeds by the end of 2025.

Difficult to Estimate Amount of Invention-Related Income Likely to Be Generated. To the
extent CIRM funds new projects that result in licensed and commercialized products, the state
would receive a portion of the resulting revenue. The amount of revenue received for this
purpose is uncertain. Many times, research does not lead to an invention, but, in a few cases,
inventions do result and are lucrative. Also, a significant amount of time typically elapses from
an initial research project to commercializing an associated invention. To date, the state has
collected only a few hundred thousand dollars in invention-related income. Past revenue
collections, however, might not be a good indicator of future revenue for the reasons cited above.
Other Possible Fiscal Effects. The measure could result in numerous other indirect effects
on state and local governments. For example, to the extent the measure results in new treatments
that are more cost-effective than existing treatments, state and local governments could
experience savings in some programs such as Medi-Cal, the state’s subsidized health care
program for low-income people. The magnitude of these and other indirect effects is unknown.

effects:
 State costs of $7.8 billion to pay off principal ($5.5 billion) and interest ($2.3 billion)
on the bonds. Associated average annual debt payments of about $310 million for
25 years. The costs could be higher or lower than these estimates depending on
factors such as the interest rate and the period of time over which the bonds are

Myths vs Facts
Get the facts on Prop 38. Learn what the initiative will do and find answers to some of the most common questions about Prop 38.
Updated October 26, 2026
Can California afford Prop 38?
Fact: Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#accountability). 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go back to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), covering both the principal and the interest of the bonds. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most prevalent diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses for Californians by tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses and lower insurance premiums.
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits. Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on saving lives.
For the millions of families that are facing life-threatening and life-altering diseases that take away our loved ones, we can’t afford NOT to invest in promising cures .
Why does California need Prop 38 when the federal government funds medical research too?
Fact: Prop 38 responds to massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty that are shutting down life-saving medical research (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) at California universities and research institutes. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can’t afford to wait.
Prop 38 creates a stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts to accelerate the pace of discoveries to help the tens of millions of patients fighting cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other debilitating diseases.
Prop 38 will make California a national leader in breakthrough medical research , fostering collaboration between leading California-based universities, scientists and physicians.
Prop 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs . Scientific research has become a critical economic engine in California, and studies show (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf) that each dollar invested in medical research returns three dollars back into our state’s economy.
Does half of Prop 38 funding go to one research institute?
Fact: Half of Prop 38 funding will support a world-class nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California with access to leading scientists, technology, laboratory equipment, patients and clinical trials necessary to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.
The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy will very likely apply for funding and meet qualification requirements. However, state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific named institute (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-12/) but can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. Ultimately, the California Department of Public Health is charged with determining which institute receives the funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm).
Will scientists or politicians decide which research Prop 38 funds?
Fact: Under Prop 38, scientists and researchers oversee a competitive process to ensure the most qualified research with life-saving potential is awarded funding. Prop 38 establishes an Advisory and Accountability Research Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), composed of members from seven University of California campuses and 10 – 15 members from California nonprofit universities and academic and research institutions. Each member of the council will be a physician, scientist or researcher with demonstrated experience in the field of immunology and immunotherapy.
Should the private sector fund this research instead of Prop 38?
Fact: Public funding like Prop 38 is vital to support medical research. More than 99% of new FDA-approved drugs from 2010 to 2019 were built on publicly funded research. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2804378) Prop 38 builds on this proven model by supporting universities and nonprofit researchers to move discoveries from the lab to patients faster and more cost-effectively.
Will the people funding Prop 38 benefit financially?
Fact: Prop 38 is funded by a doctor and philanthropists who will not benefit financially. Only public universities and nonprofit research institutions in California are eligible to receive research funding.
YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocates (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses AssociationCalifornia, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson’s Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, as well as patients, doctors and researchers because it will accelerate life-saving cures. This is a publicly accountable, voter-approved bond.

Dear Attorney General Becerra:
Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed statutory initiative
(A.G. File No. 19-0022, Amendment #1) that would authorize $5.5 billion in general obligation
bonds for stem cell research and enact various changes to the California Institute for
Regenerative Medicine (CIRM).
Background
Researchers Use Stem Cells to Study and Treat Various Diseases. Stem cells are certain
types of cells that exist within humans. Researchers are interested in these types of cells for their
potential to regenerate lost cells, tissues, and organs. The field of medicine that uses stem cells
and other techniques for this purpose is known as “regenerative medicine.” One well-known
example of a regenerative medicine procedure is a bone marrow transplant. Under this
procedure, the bone marrow of a donor (which contains stem cells) is transferred to another
patient to replenish lost blood cells, typically due to certain types of cancer. Scientists are
researching the use of stem cells to treat many other diseases and health conditions.
Voters Established State Stem Cell Research Program. In 2004, voters approved
Proposition 71, which gave researchers in California a constitutional right to conduct stem cell
research. The measure also created a new state program to fund stem cell research projects,
research facilities, and other related activities. In tandem, it created a new entity, CIRM, to
administer the program. The measure also established a CIRM oversight structure, which
includes (1) a 29-member governing board responsible for making funding decisions and
adopting relevant policies, (2) three working groups responsible for advising the governing
board, and (3) a five-member committee responsible for providing independent oversight over
CIRM’s finances.
Voters Approved $3 Billion in General Obligation Bonds for Stem Cell Program. To fund
stem cell grants and CIRM’s operations, the measure authorized the state to sell general
obligation bonds. State general obligation bonds are a form of borrowing. The state sells the
bonds to investors, and the proceeds of these sales provide funding to CIRM. The state sells the
Hon. Xavier Becerra 2 December 2, 2019
bonds when CIRM needs the funds (typically once a round of grant awardees has been selected).
Once the bonds are sold to investors, the state begins repaying the investors with interest by
making annual payments over time. Proposition 71 did not specify the length of the repayment
period for each bond issuance, but the state tended to repay the bonds over ten years.
Proposition 71 bonds were taxable and a ten-year repayment period is common for these types of
bonds. (For taxable bonds, the interest that investors earn is not exempt from federal taxes.)
CIRM Has Spent Nearly All Available Funds. As Figure 1 shows, bonds issued under
Proposition 71 have comprised virtually all of CIRM’s funding, with a relatively small amount
of funding coming from investment income, private donations, and other sources. CIRM has
spent most of the available funding on grants, with smaller amounts spent on CIRM’s operations
and bond costs (discussed later in this letter). As of October 2019, all but $132 million of
CIRM’s funding has been spent. According to CIRM staff, the remaining funding will be used
primarily to oversee active grants.
Grants Have Funded Several Different Purposes. As Figure 2 (on the next page) shows,
CIRM has awarded about 75 percent of grant funds for specific research projects, including
clinical trials. The remaining 25 percent of grant funds have supported research facility
construction and equipment, related activities (for example, establishing a network of
laboratories dedicated to implementing human clinical trials), and various education initiatives
(for example, research internships for undergraduate students). The University of California has
received the greatest amount of grant funding, followed by nonprofit universities and institutions
(such as Stanford University).
CIRM Is Reducing Staffing Levels. Under Proposition 71, CIRM could spend no more than
3 percent of bond proceeds on its general administrative costs and no more than 3 percent to
Hon. Xavier Becerra 3 December 2, 2019
administer grants. At full implementation, CIRM reports having over 50 full-time equivalent
staff. As it nears the end of its programmatic funding, it has reduced operations. Currently,
CIRM employs 35 full-time equivalent staff.
CIRM Used a Small Share of Bond Proceeds for Interest Payments. Typically, the state
makes regular payments on general obligation bonds from the state General Fund. Proposition 71
required the state to take a somewhat different approach. For the first five years after receiving
voter approval, the measure required CIRM to repay interest using the bonds’ proceeds.
According to CIRM, a total of about $70 million of bond proceeds were spent on interest costs
from 2004 through 2009. In 2010, the state began paying the remaining principal and interest
from the General Fund. Currently, the state is spending $327 million annually from the General
Fund to make debt payments on Proposition 71 bonds.
Small Amount of Funding Spent on Bond Issuance Costs. Typically, certain administrative
and legal costs are associated with a bond issuance. Proposition 71 specified that bond proceeds
were to cover these administrative costs. CIRM reports using $2.6 million in bond proceeds for
these costs.
Grant Recipients Have Contributed Matching Funds to Their Projects. Many of CIRM’s
programs require a match from grant recipients. The amount of funding that applicants must
match varies by program. To cover their match, grants recipients can rely on a number of
different fund sources, including philanthropic donations, federal grants, and industry
contributions. Many recipients raise more funding than required. According to CIRM, grant
recipients report collecting a combined $4.1 billion in matching funds since 2004.

Grantees Are Required to Share Invention-Related Income With the State. Some stem cell
research is expected to lead to new inventions, including new medical technology and
treatments. Proposition 71 established an expectation that grant recipients share a portion of the
income resulting from licensing or commercializing these inventions with the state. The state’s
share of the income is deposited into the state General Fund (the state’s main operating account),
which is available to support any state program. Over the years, CIRM’s governing board has
developed specific revenue-sharing policies. Since 2004, grant recipients have contributed
$352,560 in total invention-related income to the state.
Proposal
Authorizes $5.5 Billion in Bonds for Stem Cell Activities. The proposed measure would
authorize new bonds to fund additional grants and CIRM operations. As Figure 3 (see next
page) shows, the measure limits the amount of funds CIRM can spend on its operations. In
addition, the measure sets aside a portion of bond funds for certain grant programs, such as
grants for research projects that are aimed at developing treatments and cures for diseases
affecting the brain and nervous system. For a few of these programs, CIRM’s governing board
would be required to prioritize grant applications that offer matching funds and ensure grant
awardees are distributed across the state.

the amount of bonds the state could sell each year, with the goal of spreading bond sales over at
least a ten-year period. For the first five years after the measure is enacted, bond proceeds would
cover any interest payments on the issued bonds. Beginning January 1, 2026, the state would pay
all remaining debt from the General Fund. The State Treasurer would decide the period over
which to repay the bonds, with a maximum repayment period of 40 years.

working group of national experts would advise CIRM’s governing board on ways to improve
access and affordability. Furthermore, the measure would require any revenue earned from
revenue-sharing agreements to be used to offset patient costs for regenerative medicine
treatments.
